Hi folks! My colleagues at Anthropic just announced a formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem using Lean.

Claude completed the proof in 11 days, producing computer-verifiable proofs of 30,300 theorems along the way (using 29,500 in the final proof). It’s 13 million lines of Lean code; far more than a human could reasonably write or even read in a few weeks. The finished proof compiles using just Lean’s three standard axioms. A comparator run confirmed that the theorem’s statement matches Mathlib’s own statement of FLT. 

Here’s a visualization of the proof process:

fltvideo.mp4

At the invitation of Kevin Buzzard, folks from Anthropic will be hanging out in #FLT to answer questions and discuss the project. I encourage using several topics here to keep the discussion organized.
Do you plan to do anything with the code?
(the code is here https://github.com/anthropics/fermats-last-theorem )
Also did they formalise your more modern proof or the original one?
They formalized the OG proof (well, the Darmon--Diamond--Taylor version). I say epsilon more about this in my blog post https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/09/04/flt-anthropic-has-beaten-me-to-it/

In particular they prove that the Frey curve has no point of order p>=17, they prove Langlands--Tunnell etc. Probably the best way of easily getting a feeling of what is going on is to clone the repo and then open html/index.html in a browser.

Compiling the code is another matter :-) It took me over 4 hours on a machine with 96 cores. I also ran comparator on the codebase and it took 11 hours (comparator is single-threaded!) and most of the time it was using over 250G of ram.
Yeah I think figuring out a way to do comparator multithreaded while preserving its soundness seems like a good idea, now that projects of this size are possible.

An aside: I also have the distinct impression that Fable 5.1 is capable of writing much better Lean code than its predecessors. I've recently made public QuadraticIterates, a full formalization of my first published paper (nothing to do with FLT, though). In the last few days (since Fable 5.1 became available), I had it go through all of the code and improve it, with little extra input besides some general guidelines. You can look at the resulting code (this is just 4000 lines of code) to get an impression. I, at least, was quite positively surprised.
Files like this one in the repo have two surpringly long (and weird) lines, but I wonder whether this is part of the prove2.me set-up somehow.

The video linked at the start of the thread seems to say so

Yeah so it was the key to this part of the process:

  1. Maintaining a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of theorem statements that agents used to decide what proofs they should attempt next. This was particularly helpful for mitigating memory degradation and allowing multiple agents to work in parallel.

Basically, Prove2Me served as the database for what had already been proven and thus could be used when proving something else.

Tim: I don't think nearly anyone doubted that FLT was false, but I did wonder if there were "slip-ups" - like, a lemma in a paper that was false as stated (for some not-entirely trivial reason, like maybe they write "all primes" and it was really "all primes >= 5", but this is all that was needed); or maybe the proof in that lemma is slightly wrong (the lemma says "all primes", and it's true for all primes, but the p=2 case needs a different argument, but that argument is very easy to find once you see the odd case). I would be very curious to hear about any such cases Claude ran into along the way.

Such "missteps" that are "incidentally" fixed by LLMs in the process of autoformalization have already happened a few times in other projects, but unfortunately LLMs often don't bother so much bubbling these observations to the surface. (The proof obligation here is done - move on!) I'm sure there have been more that were missed. It really only becomes visible, usually, when a human reads the whole formalization and compares to the literature. Which is not likely to happen soon, here. :)

Would Anthropic consider running some further trawling through the logs to try to spot any such places? Others could in principle try to do so, but Anthropic actually has all of the work logs and thinking tokens, so is infinitely better positioned to offer this service to the mathematical community.

If humans had completed this project, I would expect them to have learned a lot about the underlying mathematics: For example, they probably would have found some errors in the literature and fixed them in the formalization, or cases when the literature had an overly complicated argument that could be simplified, or learned more nebulous things. Of course when Kevin's EPSRC project team complete their version I expect them to find out a lot of this type. Because "What set-theoretic axioms are needed for the proof of Fermat's last theorem" is such a classic question, it seems it would be interesting to investigate that using this proof: To state some theory of relatively low consistency strength and have an AI go through the proof line-by-line and verify every step can be adapted to work in this theory. I know that there are ideas (like this approach suggested by Joel David Hamkins https://mathoverflow.net/a/28913/18060) for how to do that in set theory. I don't know what can be done along the same lines but closer to Lean's type theory. (Of course, I wouldn't be surprised at this point if AIs are capable of translating the whole proof into some set-theoretic proof assistant.)
This is the motivation behind my question. But even if the proof stays in Type it lives in an axiomatic system where Type 37 exists, so I am not sure what we may deduce.

If all the theorems can be instantiated without leaving Type, that does imply that the large cardinal axioms associated to universes were unnecessary, no? Or is it trickier than that because the logical correspondence to ZFC isn't "one-to-one" with the large cardinal axioms somehow?

the type universes are in one-to-one correspondence with inaccessibles in ZFC. Having only Type 0 and nothing above is consistent with ZFC + exactly 1 inaccessible. If you get rid of Type 0, you are left with the calculus of constructions, which is a bit like higher order arithmetic.

Angus Macintyre's appendix to Chapter 1 ("The Impact of Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems on Mathematics") of Kurt Gödel and the Foundations of Mathematics: Horizons of Truth (Cambridge University Press, 2011) sketches how one might prove FLT in PA. Some people would be interested in knowing whether MacIntyre's sketch can really be fleshed out in detail. My impression, however, is that this isn't the kind of question that is easy for current proof assistants to tackle. Not to say that they couldn't tackle it, but they're not really designed to address "reverse mathematics" questions. I think it's not even that easy to confirm mechanically, from the Lean formalization, that FLT is provable in ZF (in particular, without universes).

Alex Meiburg said:

Would Anthropic consider running some further trawling through the logs to try to spot any such places?

I asked it to go through its work and there were really just a few small issues, and some potential typos.

Mennicke 1967, used for Ihara's lemma. It asserts that the Schur multiplier of SL₂(Z/m) vanishes for all m. Beyl showed in 1986 that it is Z/2 exactly when 4 divides m, and repaired Mennicke's argument. Our proof follows Beyl's repair.

Lang, Elliptic Functions, Ch. 5 Thm 3(ii), used. The symmetry of the modular polynomial is stated for all n and fails only in the degenerate case n = 1, where Lang's own proof also breaks. The Lean states it for n > 1. This is the commenter's archetype.

Jordan–Livné 1985, Lemma 5.5(2) (which they take from Kurihara), read but not used in the end. Its "conversely" half is stated for all p and fails when p ≡ 3 mod 4. It is harmless inside the paper, and I found no erratum.

Jordan–Livné 1986, Theorem 2.3, read but not used. The printed component-group formula is off by powers of 2 and 3: it gives 1/6 for a group of order 1. An agent re-derived the right formula. Its note does not cite Papikian, who had published the same fix in 2016.

Edixhoven 1992, p. 583, read but not used, and the least certain of the five. One "we conclude that" appears to assert full local-localness before the argument justifies it. The theorem is fine, and a two-line reordering of the paper's own ingredients repairs the proof.

Hi, I helped build prove2.me. I would like to give some of my own perspective. Note that I am not affiliated with Anthropic nor was I involved in anything related to FLT.

First of all, prove2me is an experiment in formalization of mathematical research. We are hoping that it teaches us important lessons about the future of mathematics. The intent here is to benefit the mathematical community at large.

To use prove2me, one can submit a target theorem statement (for now, in Lean), or help prove such a target theorem statement [a]. It is designed to be collaborative. In fact, we designed an architecture we thought would allow a large number of humans and agents to work together when proving a single target theorem statement.

Let me describe the architecture, as I suspect it was crucial to Anthropic's success here. The main idea is to use a "top-down programming" perspective on theorem proving. When working on a theorem, one can submit either a full proof, or a "proof sketch", aka a formal implication from a number of (possibly unproven) lemmas to the theorem. Each of these lemmas can then be worked on by you or by some other prove2me user. Of course they can submit a "proof sketch" to a lemma, and this process can recurse as many times as necessary. This creates a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that can grow quite large. Note that there may be several "proof sketches" for any statement, but only one of them has to succeed for the statement to be proven.

I have not seen this architecture in other formalization sites or projects. I think it has two key advantages when proving theorems with a large number of provers [b]:

  1. A prover can work on any node in the DAG, which reduces duplicate effort. It is easier to suggest a proof strategy and submit a "proof sketch" than to prove something outright. This increases the number of nodes, and thus the number of statements a prover can work on. Of course, provers can simultaneously work on different "proof sketches" for the same statement, just as human provers may try different proof strategies.
  2. A prover does not need to compile the whole proof, which dramatically improves runtime and memory requirements. It only has to compile its proof or "proof sketch" of the statement it is working on. This is because we store proofs and "proof sketches" directly in a database. In other projects like mathlib, multiple statements and proofs can live in the same file, so edits (I think) require recompiling more than just the thing you are working on.

It would be great for others to try out prove2me. We have many goals with the site, including (1) giving researchers a public place to share formalizations of their work and (2) understanding how humans and agents can collaboratively solve and formalize new mathematics [c]. That being said, autoformalization of this type presents obvious risks to human understanding, and so we are thinking about how to incentivize explainability and interpretability. It is also possible to prove the same target statement many times over, so prove2me could be a place to explore canonicalization. We're especially open to any ideas in these directions.

[a] We call them "missions" in the spirit of NASA missions.
[b] In this situation, a "swarm" of agents.
[c] This is directly inspired by projects like polymath.

There are several axes for classifying review-aiding tools.

  • Some tools suggest something is wrong and should be changed (or actually suggest specific changes to code directly), while others just provide information that can help humans decide if the code is as intended. For example, linters are a deterministic tool that suggest something is wrong and should be changed (or have the linter disabled locally if appropriate). The tools that report new and changed declarations and changes to numbers of imports are also a deterministic tool, but they don't say that anything is wrong, they just provide information that's expected to be useful to both the PR submitter and reviewers.
  • Some tools are fully deterministic; some are AI-based. If something can be fully deterministic, it's probably best to implement it that way.
  • Some tools are sufficiently reliable and useful to be worth surfacing their output (whether suggesting something is wrong, or just providing information) by default. Some are less reliable, or require more expertise to assess their output, and in these cases it may be more useful to have a way for a reviewer (if they think that tool would be helpful to their review of that PR) to run the tool, see the output and then select which parts of the output to surface for attention by the PR author, rather than the author seeing all of it by default. This applies to deterministic tools as well as AI-based ones. For example, deterministic tools for automatic golfing may suggest changes where a particular tactic can shorten a proof but it's necessary to judge whether they are desirable (maybe rfl works in a particular place but using it is not a good design choice there; maybe even a change that makes sense on its own should not be applied to existing code being refactored or moved by a PR), and so surfacing their suggestions by default for a beginner may not be a good idea.
